 SNAP recipients push back on junk-food ban with lawsuit claiming health benefits for diabetes, autism 
 By 
 Emily Lang 
 Published 
 Nov. 20, 2026, 4:02 p.m. ET 
 See more of our coverage in your search results. 
 Make New York Post a Preferred Source 
 Recipients of SNAP benefits are suing the U.S. government over its restrictions on junk-food purchases like soda and candy — with some plaintiffs claiming they need the snacks to regulate medical conditions including diabetes. 
 The National Center for Law and Economic Justice filed a proposed federal class-action lawsuit on behalf of seventeen individuals and one convenience store association against the U.S. Department of Agriculture after the agency encouraged states to submit SNAP Food Restriction Waivers that prohibit certain items across 18 states from being purchased with government assistance. 
 A sign indicates SNAP EBT acceptance inside a CVS store in Paramus, NJ, on Wednesday, Oct. 5, 2022. Christopher Sadowski 
 While the restrictions vary across states, the majority of them include candy, sodas, and some include prepared packaged foods. 
 Advertisement
 Plaintiffs who are diabetics say they need quick access to candy in order to raise their blood-sugar levels and are cut off from being able to make purchases with their monthly benefits, which average $344 per household.
 One plaintiff, Tamara Wagner of Fargo, North Dakota, has been disabled most of her life, according to court documents. She has diabetes and a condition that gives her an irregular heartbeat which she claims she needs a drink like Gatorade to regulate.

 Wagner also experiences nausea while eating and relies on diet soda to relieve it. With the state’s new waiver, she is unable to purchase items and has been rationing them in addition to experiencing significant nausea and bloating, according to the suit.
 Advertisement
 The lawsuit is hoping to immediately remove the restrictions and block their enforcement. No damages are being sought. Earlier this year, a judge blocked the Trump administration from banning junk food and in March five states sued over the ban as well. 
 “These unlawful waivers serve as a backdoor method to restrict access to SNAP,” Katharine Deabler-Meadows, senior attorney with the National Center, said in a statement to the Indiana Capital Chronicle. 
 “Our lawsuit seeks to hold the Trump administration accountable for violating the law and causing unprecedented chaos for SNAP recipients and retailers alike.” 
 When the program was announced last year, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy praised the state waivers.  
 Advertisement
 “For years, SNAP has used taxpayer dollars to fund soda and candy — products that fuel America’s diabetes and chronic disease epidemics,” said Kennedy said at the time. “These waivers help put real food back at the center of the program and empower states to lead the charge in protecting public health.”
 A Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program Food Stamps Accepted sign is displayed at a gas station food market in Fort Lee, NJ, on July 15, 2023. Christopher Sadowski 
 But the waivers have sparked unintended consequences, according to the lawsuit.
 Kathryn Fitzpatrick of Montana has autism and ADHD, according to court documents, and claims that cooking is very difficult because of her attention disorders and can’t process things when she is very hungry. Under Montana’s waiver, food items like prepared desserts, candy, energy drinks and high-sugar beverages are restricted.
 Advertisement
 A man in North Dakota, James Ness, claims he relies on gum and mints to address his post-traumatic stress disorder and doesn’t have other funds to make the purchases without benefits, according to the suit. A woman in Virginia, Kim Kovarikova, claims she relies on caffeine-free root beer, adding that she “struggles to drink enough water to stay hydrated.”
